hypotheses.impact: latestVersion regression → latest()/at() returning stale/wrong data; incorrect fee carryover in future _commitRequested (it reads _responses[_global.latestVersion]).
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce `version.timestamp > _global.latestVersion` before assignment in commit(), or in _commitRequested.

hypotheses.title: MetaQuantsFactory._parsePrices is view but depends on msg.value not validated for sufficient fee
hypotheses.description: Unlike PythFactory, MetaQuantsFactory._parsePrices verifies signatures off-chain but never charges or forwards any update fee; more importantly, it accepts `data` that is `abi.decode`d into `UpdateAndSignature[]` and verifies each signature against the immutable `signer` with no freshness/replay protection (there is no nonce, expiry, or publish-time check against `version`). The KeeperFactory.commit path later calls `_validatePrices(version, prices)` to check publishTime, but the signature itself can be replayed across identical payloads and there's no check that signed data matches the specific `version`/underlying beyond the id.
hypotheses.attackPath: A keeper or attacker who obtained any previously signed `UpdateAndSignature` for that id/publishTime can resubmit the exact same `data` (signature still valid) at the same or a later commit for the same version timestamp; if `_validatePrices` only checks against `version` and publishTime 0 it may pass. Replay of a stale signed payload could set an outdated price.
hypotheses.impact: Potential stale-price acceptance / replay of signed updates leading to incorrect settlement prices.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind signed payloads to the specific version/underlying and enforce freshness (publishTime vs. version) with explicit rejection of already-used signatures (nonce or timestamp window).

hypotheses.title: KeeperOracle.settle iterates callbacks and pays asyncFee per callback without checking receiver/market.settle success ordering side effects
hypotheses.description: `settle` reads `priceResponse.asyncFee` fresh on every loop iteration and pushes it for each callback. Because `settle` requires `_global.latestVersion >= version` and callbacks are removed one-by-one, an account whose `market.settle` internally re-requests a settlement callback for the same version (via `oracle.request` → `KeeperOracle.request` → `_localCallbacks[currentTimestamp].add(account)`) can re-add itself to the same set while the loop is iterating (`callbacks.at(0)`/`callbacks.remove(account)`). Since the loop continues until `maxCount` is reached or the set is empty, a re-adding callback can cause extra iterations beyond the intended count of distinct accounts and drain extra `asyncFee`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker registers account A as callback for version V. 2. On each settle(A) call the market re-requests and re-adds A to `_localCallbacks[V]`, so `callbacks.length()` stays > 0. 3. Loop keeps executing while `i < maxCount`, paying `asyncFee` each iteration to the receiver.
hypotheses.impact: Over-payment of async settlement fees to the receiver, draining the factory token balance / fee pool.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot the callback list to a fixed array before iterating and do not re-read the live set, or track a per-iteration cap on distinct accounts.

hypotheses.title: `Oracle.at()` loop skips index 0 and stops at `i > 0`, so the first epoch is unreachable
hypotheses.description: `for (uint256 i = _global.current - 1; i > 0; i--)` iterates while `i > 0`, meaning `i == 1` is the lowest iteration but the backwards scan stops before checking the actual first epoch at index `oracles[0]` equivalent. If `current` is 1, the loop never runs (goes to else), and it uses `oracles[_global.current].provider`, missing a timestamp that belongs to epoch 0. However, more importantly, the loop's break condition `timestamp > uint256(oracles[i].timestamp)` breaks at the *first* older epoch, returning the current provider even when the timestamp belongs to that older epoch's range (since `at` should descend into epochs where `timestamp <= oracles[i].timestamp`). The loop must continue descending while `timestamp <= oracles[i].timestamp`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Oracle is updated to a new provider; a user queries `at(timestamp)` for a historical version still within the previous epoch. The loop breaks at `i=current-1` if `timestamp > oracles[current-1].timestamp` is false; it then tries `oracles[current-1].provider` — but the break logic is reversed: it should break when `timestamp > oracles[i].timestamp` (in the past go down), so it does, but `oracles[i].timestamp` is the *current* epoch's start timestamp, not the boundary. In fact with multiple hops, queries for versions committed in intermediate epochs can be answered by the wrong provider (latest).
hypotheses.impact: Wrong historical versions/receipts returned to markets for settlement, causing incorrect settlement fees and payouts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Iterate `i = _global.current; i > 0; i--` with boundary `timestamp > oracles[i-1].timestamp` comparing epoch boundaries, and use `oracles[i-1].provider` correctly.

hypotheses.title: `_parsePrices` in MetaQuantsFactory verifies signatures per-update but permits cross-feed replay/reorder via id bind to array index
hypotheses.description: `_parsePrices` iterates `updates` and for each checks `_verifySignature`. It then requires `parsedUpdate.priceFeed.id == underlyingIds[i]` — binding update `i` to the `i`-th passed underlying id. The signed payload is only `updates[i].encodedUpdate`, which contains the priceFeed id and price. Since each update is signed independently and includes its feed id, an attacker cannot substitute a different feed, but they can *reorder* the `updates` array relative to `underlyingIds`. However, the binding checks `underlyingIds[i]`, so if the caller reorders both in tandem it's still the same feed. The real issue: there is no `publishTime` monotonicity check in `_parsePrices` itself (the caller `_validatePrices` is responsible, but `_parsePrices` returns records with arbitrary publishTime and price from independently signed messages). If the same signature is replayed with a later `version`, the factory's `_validatePrices` (declared but not shown) may or may not reject. Since signatures aren't bound to `msg.sender`, version, or chain-id, anyone can replay a signed update to any version accepted by validation.
hypotheses.attackPath: A keeper obtains a valid signed `encodedUpdate` (publicly constructible from the signed message). They submit it as part of `factory.commit(...)` with an arbitrary `version` argument that passes `_validatePrices` — the signature check passes because it only checks the update payload, not `version`.
hypotheses.impact: Replay of prices to versions where they don't belong; stale price could be committed as a valid oracle version, distorting settlement.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `version`, `underlyingId`, and `chainId` in the signed message and verify them; reject reuse of the same `encodedUpdate` on-chain via nonce/timestamp tracking.

hypotheses.title: MetaQuantsFactory signature does not bind to oracle id/exponent, enabling cross-feed and exponent manipulation of parsed prices
hypotheses.description: `_verifySignature(updates[i].encodedUpdate, updates[i].signature)` recovers the signer over the encoded update, and then `parsedUpdate.priceFeed.id` is compared to `underlyingIds[i]`. So the update is bound to a feed id by the signer, but the loop does not bind each signed update to the position/id it is being used for beyond the decoded `id` check. A signed update can be replayed against any version/commit call (there is no nonce, version, timestamp, or expiry binding in `_parsePrices`), and `publishTime` is taken from the update, feeding `PriceRecord`. Additionally `_parsePrices` is declared `view` here but the override in this contract omits `override` on the Pyth side; in MetaQuants the `view` mutability allows the signer to be deterministic — the real issue is replay: the same signed update can be reused in any transaction and any version as long as `priceFeed.id` matches, with no binding to the version being committed.
hypotheses.attackPath: Capture any valid signed update (public mempool / calldata). Replay it in `commit` for a later version; `_validatePrices` accepts it if `publishTime` matches the requested version (attacker may need a matching-time signed update but can reuse one signed for a time equal to the target). Because no per-commit nonce/version is included in the signed payload, the protocol cannot distinguish a stale replay from a fresh update.
hypotheses.impact: Stale or replayed prices can be committed, and combined with an arbitrary `publishTime` chosen by the signer-signed payload the validation window can be bypassed in some configurations; mispricing of market versions.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include version/timestamp/chainId/contract address (and ideally a nonce) inside the signed message, and validate that `parsedUpdate`'s bound version matches `version` in `_parsePrices`.

hypotheses.title: PythFactory._parsePrices passes all ids in one parse call and single data blob; length mismatch between parsedPrices and underlyingIds unhandled
hypotheses.description: `_parsePrices` builds `datas` with exactly one element (`datas[0] = data`) and passes `underlyingIds` (length N) as the price id list to `pyth.parsePriceFeedUpdates`. It then iterates `parsedPrices.length` and writes `prices[i]`. If `pyth` returns fewer feeds than `underlyingIds` (e.g., because the single encoded update blob only contains updates for a subset of ids), `prices` has entries left as default (zero) — there is no check that `parsedPrices.length == underlyingIds.length`. Those zero `PriceRecord`s have `publishTime == 0`, `price == 0`, which `_validatePrices` (not shown) may reject, but a default zero price could also be accepted depending on validation; more concretely, the `updateFee` is computed once and assigned to every record, but `msg.value` may have paid for a different number of updates than N, and the surplus/deficit accounting is not checked here.
hypotheses.attackPath: Caller supplies a `data` blob whose embedded update count is less than `underlyingIds.length`; `parsePriceFeedUpdates` returns fewer feeds; `prices` contains zero-default records for the tail. Depending on downstream `_validatePrices`, either commit reverts (DoS) or zero prices are used.
hypotheses.impact: DoS or acceptance of zero/default prices for tail ids.
hypotheses.recommendation: Assert `parsedPrices.length == underlyingIds.length` and revert otherwise; validate each record's publishTime/price is non-zero before returning.

hypotheses.title: MultiInvoker._update leaves withdraw of positive balanceBack to DSU as withdraw to account even for negative-collateral path
hypotheses.description: In _update, collateral sign == 1 triggers _deposit. After market.update, withdrawAmount = Fixed6Lib.from(balanceAfter - balanceBefore). If negative collateral is passed, market.update pushes |collateral| DSU to MultiInvoker, so DSU balance increases; withdrawAmount positive; _withdraw(account, withdrawAmount.abs(), wrap). That correctly forwards. If collateral has a positive sign and _deposit pulls DSU, balanceBefore is taken BEFORE _deposit. Wait — balanceBefore is recorded before the deposit. After _deposit, DSU balance decreases by amount, then market.update pulls collateral from MultiInvoker, so DSU decreases further. withdrawAmount will be negative, so isZero false, and it withdraws abs() from MultiInvoker to account. If there is residual DSU from prior runs or stuck balances in the contract, that could be withdrawn to the account and drained. But since MultiInvoker is publicly invoked by anyone with operator permission, an operator could pass `collateral` with a value that causes a net positive delta in the invoker and forwards it to the account. However, DSU.balanceOf() in _update is the contract-wide balance, not per-account, so any residual DSU in the contract could be swept to msg.sender's account. That is a real concern if the contract can accumulate dust (e.g., leftover from shortfall between deposit and update). Under normal usage, the amount is exactly bal.
hypotheses.attackPath: If the invoker holds stray DSU (from any prior incomplete flow, dust, direct transfers), an operator could construct an invocation sequence where the delta is positive and pull those funds to their account.
hypotheses.impact: Sweeping of stray DSU.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute deltas only around the specific deposit/withdraw for that update and assert the exact amount, or restrict sweeps. But primarily do not rely on total DSU balance delta.

hypotheses.title: RebalanceLib.checkMarket allows rebalance when groupCollateral <= 0 producing target of zero and draining surplus markets
hypotheses.description: `targetCollateral = groupCollateral.mul(marketConfig.target)` may be negative when total group collateral is negative (e.g., markets in deficit). The code then computes `pctFromTarget = 1 - marketCollateral/targetCollateral`; if `targetCollateral` is negative and `marketCollateral` positive, `marketCollateral.div(targetCollateral)` is a negative ratio, `pctFromTarget` > 1, threshold check passes, and `imbalance = targetCollateral - marketCollateral` becomes strongly negative. In `_rebalanceGroup`, negative imbalances pull collateral from markets with positive collateral. Meanwhile groups with any target 0 (checked earlier in the zero-target branch) and any market with surplus will be pulled even if the group total is not actually imbalanced in a beneficial way; there is no guard preventing `checkMarket` from returning `canRebalance = true` when it should not, so `_rebalanceGroup` can be called permissionlessly (no signature required) and move collateral between markets out of the owner's intended allocation.
hypotheses.attackPath: A keeper configures markets with one market deficit and another surplus, or with all targets positive, and calls `rebalanceGroup(owner, group)` permissionlessly. `_settleMarkets` runs, `checkGroup` computes imbalances from stale/rebalanced values, and the two-pass loop pulls from surplus and pushes to deficit even when the group has no net surplus — potentially pulling collateral from an actually-healthy market into a market that is already underwater or into fees, since `_rebalanceGroup` is unauthenticated.
hypotheses.impact: Permissionless keeper can move an owner's collateral between the owner's markets whenever configuration thresholds are crossed, and with negative group collateral the math can push positions to zero/deficit in ways the owner did not intend; funds can be pushed into markets that then cannot be withdrawn.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `checkMarket`, when `targetCollateral.lt(0)` treat it as fully out of balance only in a controlled way (or skip), and in `_rebalanceGroup` require that the sum of negative imbalances is at least the sum of positive imbalances before pushing collateral.

hypotheses.title: chargeFee wraps then pulls DSU; account DSU balance unpulled remains, but wrapIfNecessary shortfall ignored
hypotheses.description: `chargeFee` calls `wrapIfNecessary(transferAmount, false)` then `DSU.pullTo(account, msg.sender, transferAmount)`. If the account has USDC but the wrap produced fewer DSU than `transferAmount` (reserve fee, or part was already wrapped), `pullTo` will revert or transfer from other DSU balances. More importantly, `wrapIfNecessary` silently does nothing if the account's DSU and USDC are insufficient; the subsequent `DSU.pullTo` then reverts, making the fee charge fail. An operator then cannot collect fees if the account has no collateral, which is expected—but combined with `wrapIfNecessary` triggering a `reserve.mint` (potentially slippage/outcome dependent), an operator can attempt to charge at a moment when the reserve is favorable.
hypotheses.attackPath: Operator calls `chargeFee` repeatedly; each call wraps only if the account has USDC. Operators could avoid charging until desired.
hypotheses.impact: Minor; only relayer/keeper economics. Not fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: N/A (drop if not actionable).

hypotheses.title: _raiseKeeperFee in MultiInvoker withdraws from market without checking withdraw succeeded or remaining fee
hypotheses.description: `_raiseKeeperFee` decodes `(account, market, fee)`, computes `raisedKeeperFee = UFixed6Lib.from(keeperFee, true).min(fee)`, calls `_marketWithdraw(market, account, raisedKeeperFee)` which invokes `market.update` with a negative collateral delta, and returns `UFixed18Lib.from(raisedKeeperFee)`. The return value is assumed to be the amount actually pulled. But `market.update` may charge socialization / settlement losses causing less to actually be received, or the account's collateral may be insufficient and the update may revert. If the update succeeds but harvest does not yield the full `raisedKeeperFee` (e.g., because collateral gets applied to loss), the return value overstates what was transferred, and the Kept base may transfer more DSU than was pulled. Given the account has an approved DSU balance via `_deposit`, this could draw from account's DSU—but the account is not the msg.sender.
hypotheses.attackPath: Keeper executes an order whose account is under-water; the market withdraw may revert. If it doesn't revert but returns less due to fees, the returned amount is wrong (should match actual DSU balance delta).
hypotheses.impact: Keeper reward accounting mismatch; potentially keeper receives more DSU than withdrawn, drawing from MultiInvoker's own DSU balance (which belongs to other users' claimable fees) → cross-account theft.
hypotheses.recommendation: Measure actual DSU balance delta across `_marketWithdraw` and return `min(delta, fee)`.

hypotheses.title: Trigger order execution skips order update/settlement accounting after possibly-failing canExecute re-read
hypotheses.description: `executeOrder` re-reads the stored order via `checkOrder`, charges the interface fee with `_chargeInterfaceFee`, then calls `order.execute(market, account)` which internally calls `market.settle(account)` and `market.update(...)`. However `order.maxFee` used for keeper compensation and `order.interfaceFee` used for the interface-fee charge are read from the same in-memory copy, but the order is not marked `isSpent` until after `order.execute` succeeds. If `market.update` reverts, the whole tx reverts, so no double-spend there. The concrete problem: `_chargeInterfaceFee` computes `feeAmount` from `order.notionalValue(market, account)` which reads `market.oracle().latest()` *before* `market.settle(account)` runs inside `order.execute`. The market may have a pending (unsettled) position for the account, so `notionalValue` (via `_position` which does `market.positions` + `market.pendings`) uses pending data, but the fee is deducted by `controller.chargeFee(account, feeAmount)` from the collateral account. Because the actual executed delta matches `order.delta`, this is minor, but if the account's oracle version is stale or the price updates between the two reads, the percentage-based interface fee can be computed against a different notional than the actual order.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user places a trigger order with a percentage `interfaceFee`, then leaves a large pending order (or the oracle advances) such that `notionalValue` called by `_chargeInterfaceFee` reads a price/size different from the executed order, shifting the fee paid.
hypotheses.impact: Interface/keeper fee mispricing; small over/under-charge relative to intended notional-based fee.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the interface fee from the same post-settle position/price used for execution, e.g. settle first, then compute the fee.

hypotheses.title: checkOrder invoked inside executeOrder does not re-verify market/oracle validity, allowing stale-price execution
hypotheses.description: `executeOrder` calls `checkOrder`, which calls `order.canExecute(market.oracle().latest())`. `canExecute` only checks `latestVersion.valid` and compares `latestVersion.price` to `self.price`. It does not check `staleAfter`, and after this check the actual update goes through `market.update` which enforces staleness against `context.currentTimestamp - context.latestOracleVersion.timestamp`. If the market update would revert on stale price the tx reverts — no fund loss. The real gap: `canExecute` reads `market.oracle().latest()` (the oracle's own latest) while `market.settle`/`market.update` uses `context.latestOracleVersion` — the market's version pointer. If the oracle has advanced to a version the market hasn't yet been settled to (market settlement lags oracle), the trigger can be considered executable on a price the market hasn't consumed, then executes at the market's (older) price. The keeper is still compensated.
hypotheses.attackPath: During periods where the oracle reports a new version but the market's latest version is behind, a keeper executes a trigger order that triggers on the oracle's latest price while the market trades against the older version.
hypotheses.impact: Trigger executes at a price inconsistent with the trigger condition from the market's perspective; keeper compensation paid for what is effectively the wrong trigger evaluation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `market.settle`'s actual latest oracle version for the `canExecute` check, or settle before evaluating the trigger.

hypotheses.title: `GuaranteeLib.from` omits `notional` from `GuaranteeStorageGlobalLib.validate`, allowing storage write to truncate negative/overflow values but only for local paths
hypotheses.description: `GuaranteeStorageGlobalLib.store` calls `GuaranteeStorageLib.validate(newValue)`, which checks `orders`, `longPos`, `longNeg`, `shortPos`, `shortNeg`, `takerFee`, `orderReferral` bounds, but does NOT check `solverReferral` (a `uint64`) or `notional` (a `Fixed6`). The read code for global guarantee returns `Fixed6Lib.ZERO` for `notional` and `UFixed6Lib.ZERO` for `solverReferral`, so the missing checks are consistent with what is stored. However, `GuaranteeStorageLocalLib.store` calls the same `validate` and then separately checks `notional` and `solverReferral` bounds — but a `Guarantee` accumulated via `GuaranteeLib.add` from many local guarantees can overflow `guarantee.orders` (uint256) or `solverReferral` (summed as UFixed6) after `add`, and its subsequent `store` will silently revert via `validate`. The root concern: `validate` doesn't bound `notional` or `solverReferral`, forcing every call site to remember. A missed additional bound check would silently truncate via the encoding (the bit shift masks upper bits).
hypotheses.attackPath: A user places many orders with large `takerReferral` values; the aggregated `solverReferral`/`notional` exceed `uint64`/`int64`. Local `store` reverts, blocking further updates for that account in the checkpointed block.
hypotheses.impact: Account's order processing reverts deterministically, potentially a DoS of the account's position updates for the pending checkpoint.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move `notional` and `solverReferral` bounds checks into `GuaranteeStorageLib.validate` so every `store` path is covered, and check `add` results before persisting.

hypotheses.title: SolverVault.updateCoordinator disables/claims signer without updating only on both success
hypotheses.description: The override first calls `marketFactory.updateSigner(coordinator, false)` then `updateSigner(newCoordinator, true)`, then sets `coordinator`. If the old coordinator address is `address(0)` or the new coordinator equals the old coordinator, or if the second call reverts, the first revoke has already executed. More importantly, when `newCoordinator == coordinator`, it revokes then re-enables — acceptable — but when old `coordinator` is also the owner's signer used for other things, it revokes it globally. Also this runs even if the second call reverts, leaving the vault without a signer-enabled coordinator.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner calls `updateCoordinator` with a `newCoordinator` that causes `updateSigner` to revert on the enable path (e.g., invalid address); the disable of the old coordinator completes first, leaving the vault unable to operate signatures.
hypotheses.impact: Vault can be left without an authorized signer, breaking operations that depend on coordinator signatures until owner fixes it.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set state and enable the new signer before revoking the old one, or wrap in a single call and re-check.

hypotheses.title: update(address,Fixed6,address) lets msg.sender sign on behalf of account via authorization depending on factory
hypotheses.description: `_updateMarket(account, msg.sender, Fixed6Lib.ZERO, amount, Fixed6Lib.ZERO, referrer)` passes msg.sender as the signer, relying on `IMarketFactory.authorization(account, msg.sender, signer, referrer)` to reject unauthorized calls. That authorization contract is not in scope here, so this is flagged only if the factory does not enforce that signer==msg.sender must be an approved operator/signer; otherwise anyone can open positions against any account.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `update(victim, amount, referrer)`; if `authorization` doesn't check msg.sender against operators/signers for `account`, a position is opened on the victim's account.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized position/taker exposure attributed to victim.
hypotheses.recommendation: Confirm the factory `authorization` returns operator/signer only for approved msg.sender or require `signer == msg.sender` be verified here too, e.g. explicit check that msg.sender is `account` or an operator.

hypotheses.title: _updateMarket update(address,Fixed6,Fixed6,Fixed6,address) passes address(0) signer with no auth check in Market
hypotheses.description: This overload calls `_updateMarket(account, address(0), makerAmount, takerAmount, collateral, referrer)`, i.e., signer is the zero address. `_loadUpdateContext` then calls `factory().authorization(context.account, msg.sender, signer, orderReferrer)` with signer=address(0). Whether msg.sender is allowed to act for `account` hinges entirely on `authorization`'s handling of a zero signer. If the factory treats "no signer" as "no-check", any caller could update any account's maker/taker/collateral, including withdrawing collateral.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `update(victim, maker, taker, negativeCollateral, referrer)`; collateral is pushed to msg.sender on negative sign via `token.push(msg.sender, ...)` in `_update`. If authorization permits, attacker drains victim collateral.
hypotheses.impact: Potential theft of a victim's collateral and unauthorized position changes.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure `authorization` explicitly requires msg.sender to be the account or an operator/signer of the account when signer == address(0); otherwise enforce it in Market.
